ManyBabies Habituation Project

This project aims to explore infant habituation through looking times using a large harmonised dataset from ManyBabies 1, ManyBabies 3, and ManyBabies 4. Study-relevant materials can be found on the Open Science Framework: https://osf.io/8xm4r

1 RQ1 - Shape of habituation curve

Explore which functional forms best capture habituation trajectories.

1.1 Prepare Data

# libraries
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lme4)
library(splines)
library(broom.mixed)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(mgcv)
library(gratia)
library(Matrix) # package for lme4
library(pbkrtest) # package for parametric bootstrapping test
library(lme4) #package for performing linear mixed models
library(languageR) #package for tidyverse
library(car) #Provide variance inflation factor and package to extract p values
library(MuMIn) # report marginal and condition R2 values for variance explained 
library(tidyverse) # to make tidy data, access pipes and make graphs
library(ggpubr) #To make graphs on multiple panels
library(reshape2)#package for tidyverse
library(rlang) # package for tidyverse
library(simr) #package to assess power
library(broom.mixed) #provide tidy model outputs
library(afex) #for p-values
library(viridis)#for colourblind friendly images
library(splines)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggeffects)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(emmeans)
library(splines)
library(performance) # For R-squared and model checks
library(sjPlot)      # For standardized coefficient tables
library(patchwork)   # For multi-panel distribution plots

# set environment

# read CSV
data <- read.csv("final_merged_manybabies.csv")

# assign factors
data <- data %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

# harmonize two age-variables into one
unique(data$age_group_new)
max(data$age_days)

data <- data %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    age = cut(
      age_days,
      breaks = c(0, 90, 180, 270, 365, 455, 545, 635, 653),  # boundaries in days
      labels = c(
        "< 3 months",
        "3–6 months",
        "6–9 months",
        "9–12 months",
        "12–15 months",
        "15–18 months",
        "18–21 months",
        "21 + months"
      ),
      right = FALSE
    )
  )

data <- data %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    age = dplyr::coalesce(age_group_new, age)
  )

data <- data %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    age = factor(age, levels = c(
      "< 3 months",
      "3–6 months",
      "6–9 months",
      "9–12 months",
      "12–15 months",
      "15–18 months",
      "18–21 months",
      "21 + months"
    ))
  )

# create variable with only testing trials (Training trials [-2, -1, 0] are excluded because they serve familiarization purposes and are not relevant for the main outcome) 
data <- data %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    testing_trial = ifelse(trial_number > 0, trial_number, NA)
  )

# log-transform data (The log transformation is useful because looking times are usually skewed, and scaling helps especially when fitting random slopes and GAMs.)
data <- data %>% 
  mutate(
    unique_subject_identifier = as.factor(unique_subject_identifier),
    lab_id = as.factor(lab_id),
    project_id = as.factor(project_id),
    log_looking_time = log1p(looking_time),
    testing_trial_sc = as.numeric(scale(testing_trial)),
    age_days_sc = as.numeric(scale(age_days))
  )

# remove NA for complete-case analysis
data_model <- data %>%
  filter(!is.na(looking_time))

# clean modelling data => final clean-up
data_model <- data %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(looking_time),
    !is.na(testing_trial),
    !is.na(unique_subject_identifier),
    !is.na(project_id),
    !is.na(lab_id)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    log_looking_time = log1p(looking_time),
    testing_trial_sc = as.numeric(scale(testing_trial))
  )

1.2 Simplify Data

We have roughly 55,000 observations. When testing new code, I can use this smaller sample so things run faster (= use data_sample). Once your code is ready, I will apply it to the full dataset (= use data).

set.seed(123)

data_sample <- data %>%
  dplyr::sample_n(5000)

1.3 Plot Overall Habituation Curve

The plot shows a steel early habituation (steep drop), which flattens at circa trial No. 4. This looks like a possible non-linear relationship!

ggplot(data, aes(x = testing_trial, y = looking_time)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line") +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = 0.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1, max(data$testing_trial, na.rm = TRUE), by = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Trial Number",
    y = "Looking Time (in seconds)",
    title = "Looking Time Across Trials"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

1.4 Create Overall Habituation Curve Models

To explore which functional forms best capture habituation trajectories, I model looking time as a function of trial number using a series of regression models. Specifically, I compare linear, quadratic, cubic and other shapes (using splines) relationships the variables.

First, I estimate a linear model to assess whether looking time decreases across trials. I then extend this model by including a quadratic term to capture potential curvature in the habituation trajectory. In addition, I fit flexible non-linear models using spline functions to allow for more complex shapes. Importantly, I always use mixed-models with infant-level random intercepts, to account for repeated measurements within infants.

model_linear_mixed <- lmer(
  log_looking_time ~ testing_trial_sc +
    (1 | project_id) +
    (1 | lab_id) +
    (1 | unique_subject_identifier),
  data = data_model,
  REML = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

model_quadratic_mixed <- lmer(
  log_looking_time ~ testing_trial_sc + I(testing_trial_sc^2) +
    (1 | project_id) +
    (1 | lab_id) +
    (1 | unique_subject_identifier),
  data = data_model,
  REML = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

model_spline_mixed <- lmer(
  log_looking_time ~ ns(testing_trial_sc, df = 3) +
    (1 | project_id) +
    (1 | lab_id) +
    (1 | unique_subject_identifier),
  data = data_model,
  REML = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

1.4.1 Linear Model

  • Looking-time decreases significantly across trials (Slope = -0.27 [95% CI -0.28, -0.27], t = -72.79), which tells us: habituation is happening.
  • On average, looking-time decreased by approximately 0.27 seconds per trial.
  • There is substantial variability in baseline looking- times across infants, supporting the inclusion of random intercepts.
  • The average looking-time in the first trial was 9.2 seconds.

1.4.2 Quadratic Model

  • There is a significant decrease in looking time across trials (Slope = -0.49 [95% CI -0.516, -0.459], t = -33.69) and a significant positive quadratic effect (b = 0.013, t = 15.33).
  • This indicates that looking-time decreased rapidly at early trials and then leveled off over time, consistent with a typical habituation trajectory.

1.4.3 Spline Model

  • There is a significant nonlinear decrease in looking time across trials.
  • Splines cannot be interpreted as easily.
  • The spline model provided the best fit to the data compared to linear and quadratic models, indicating that habituation follows a nonlinear trajectory characterized by a rapid initial decrease and subsequent leveling off. This pattern is consistent with typical habituation processes.
# A mixed-effects model using natural splines revealed.

1.4.5 Plot the selected model (spline model)

# Plot Spline Model
ggplot(data_model, aes(x = testing_trial, y = looking_time)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line") +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ splines::ns(x, df = 3),
    se = TRUE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Trial Number",
    y = "Looking Time",
    title = "Observed Habituation Pattern With Nonlinear Smooth"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
# Here, I am showing the average observed habituation pattern and overlaying a smooth model-based curve to see how well a nonlinear trajectory captures it.

# Spline Flexibility
fit_spline_models <- function(df_values, data) {
  models <- list()
  
  for (d in df_values) {
    fml <- as.formula(paste0(
      "log_looking_time ~ ns(testing_trial_sc, df = ", d, ") + ",
      "(1 | project_id) + (1 | lab_id) + (1 | unique_subject_identifier)"
    ))
    
    models[[paste0("df_", d)]] <- lmer(
      fml,
      data = data,
      REML = FALSE,
      control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
    )
  }
  
  models
}

spline_models <- fit_spline_models(1:6, data_model)

AIC_table <- data.frame(
  df = 1:6,
  AIC = sapply(spline_models, AIC),
  BIC = sapply(spline_models, BIC),
  singular = sapply(spline_models, isSingular)
)

# The sensitivity analysis showed that increasing spline flexibility improved model fit, particularly up to four degrees of freedom. After this point, improvements in BIC were small, suggesting that the main conclusion of a nonlinear habituation trajectory is robust and not dependent on one specific spline specification.

1.4.7 All models in one plot

# Observed mean looking time per trial
data_summary <- data_model %>%
  group_by(testing_trial) %>%
  summarise(mean_lt = mean(looking_time, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Prediction grid
pred_grid <- data_model %>%
  distinct(testing_trial, testing_trial_sc) %>%
  arrange(testing_trial)

# Add fixed-effect predictions from each model
pred_grid$Linear <- expm1(predict(model_linear_mixed, pred_grid, re.form = NA))
pred_grid$Quadratic <- expm1(predict(model_quadratic_mixed, pred_grid, re.form = NA))
pred_grid$Spline <- expm1(predict(model_spline_mixed, pred_grid, re.form = NA))

# Long format for plotting
pred_long <- pred_grid %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Linear, Quadratic, Spline),
    names_to = "Model",
    values_to = "pred_lt"
  )

# Plot all models
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = data_summary,
    aes(x = testing_trial, y = mean_lt),
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = pred_long,
    aes(x = testing_trial, y = pred_lt, color = Model, linetype = Model),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:16) +
  labs(
    x = "Trial Number",
    y = "Looking Time",
    title = "Predicted Habituation Trajectories by Model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
# Because the mixed models were fitted to log transformed looking time, the plotted observed values are back transformed mean log looking times. This makes the observed points comparable to the model predictions. The spline model follows the nonlinear habituation pattern best and was also preferred by AIC and BIC.

2 RQ2 - Individual differences

This section examines whether demographic variables explain individual differences in habituation trajectories. We want to identify factors that explain variability across infants.

  • 2.1 What factors moderate differences?
  • 2.2 Which moderators are most important?
  • 2.3 Do moderators relate to different aspects?
  • 2.4 Are there identifiable subgroups?

2.1 Prepare Data

data <- read_csv("final_merged_manybabies.csv")

# 1. Format text data as categories (factors) for the model
data <- data %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

# 2. Standardize Age: Create consistent categories for all infants
unique(data$age_group_new)
[1] 15–18 months 12–15 months 9–12 months  3–6 months   6–9 months  
[6] 18–21 months <NA>        
6 Levels: 12–15 months 15–18 months 18–21 months 3–6 months ... 9–12 months
max(data$age_days)
[1] 653
data <- data %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    age = cut(
      age_days,
      breaks = c(0, 90, 180, 270, 365, 455, 545, 635, 653),  # boundaries in days
      labels = c(
        "< 3 months",
        "3–6 months",
        "6–9 months",
        "9–12 months",
        "12–15 months",
        "15–18 months",
        "18–21 months",
        "> 21 months"
      ),
      right = FALSE
    )
  )

data <- data %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    age = dplyr::coalesce(age_group_new, age)
  )

data <- data %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    age = factor(age, levels = c(
      "< 3 months",
      "3–6 months",
      "6–9 months",
      "9–12 months",
      "12–15 months",
      "15–18 months",
      "18–21 months",
      "> 21 months"
    ))
  )

# 3. Focus on testing: Remove practice/warm-up trials (trial number 0 or less)
data <- data %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    testing_trial = ifelse(trial_number > 0, trial_number, NA)
  )

# 4. Standardize continuous measurements (Z-transform)
# This centers variables at 0 with a standard deviation of 1 for model stability.
data$household_size_z  <-  scale(data$household_size, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)

data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    household_size_z = as.numeric(scale(household_size, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)
                                  ),
  )

# 5. Remove trials with missing "looking time" data to ensure clean input for models

data_model <- data %>%
  filter(!is.na(looking_time)
         )

2.3 Main model: Demographic moderators of the habituation trajectory

To evaluate whether demographic variables (household size, language background, age, sex, and caregiver gender) modulate the habituation trajectory, we employed a confirmatory model-testing strategy. We first fitted a comprehensive ‘full’ model incorporating these factors as fixed effects and their interactions with the trial number (modeled via natural splines, \(df=4\)). We then utilized the drop1 procedure and AIC comparison to evaluate whether the inclusion of these parameters significantly improved model fit compared to a parsimonious baseline model (the habituation trajectory alone). This approach ensures that we do not overfit our models with demographic predictors that do not account for meaningful variance in infant looking time.

# Define all predictors you plan to use in Q2
q2_vars <- c("looking_time", "testing_trial", "unique_subject_identifier", "age",
              "participant_sex", "language_group", 
             "household_size_z", "parent1_education", "race", "project_id", "lab_id", "stimulus_id", "primarycaregiver_gender")

# Check which variables are missing
missing_q2_vars <- setdiff(q2_vars, names(data_model))
missing_q2_vars
character(0)
# add missing variable household size
data_model <- data_model %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    household_size_z = as.numeric(scale(household_size))
  )

# Create a subset with no NAs in these specific columns
data_q2_complete <- data_model %>%
  dplyr::select(all_of(q2_vars)) %>%
  na.omit()

# Check how many observations you have left
nrow(data_q2_complete)
[1] 6282
#1 Full model (using complete dataset)

# We use ns(testing_trial, 4) to maintain consistency with the Q1/Q3 spline model
model_q2_dropped <- lmer(
  log1p(looking_time) ~ ns(testing_trial, 4) * language_group + 
                        ns(testing_trial, 4) * household_size_z + 
                        age + 
                        participant_sex + 
                        primarycaregiver_gender + 
                        (1 | project_id) + (1 | lab_id) + (1 | stimulus_id) + (1 | unique_subject_identifier), 
  data = data_q2_complete, 
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# Use summary to see the results of all predictors at once
summary(model_q2_dropped)

2.4 Model comparison

We compare our hypothesis-driven “Full” model against the baseline “Reduced” model

model_comparison <- AIC(model_q2_dropped, model_q2_final)
print(model_comparison)
                 df      AIC
model_q2_dropped 26 9928.121
model_q2_final   10 9852.665

Model comparison indicates that the Reduced Model (Baseline) is superior, as evidenced by a lower AIC (9278.3) compared to the Full Model (9353.5). The higher df in the Full Model reflects the additional parameters required to test demographic predictors. Because these parameters did not substantially lower the AIC, we conclude that the demographic factors do not significantly account for variance in infant looking time beyond the established habituation trajectory.

While our baseline model (\(m0\)) effectively captures the habituation trajectory, we wanted to ensure these results hold true across different participant backgrounds. To do this, we conducted a sensitivity analysis. We took our baseline model and systematically added demographic variables—such as age, language, and household size—one by one. We then compared these expanded models against our baseline to see if the new variables actually improved our ability to predict looking times. This process allows us to confirm that the observed habituation patterns are robust and not driven by demographic differences.

2.5 Sensitivity analysis: Individual moderator tests

# 0. Base Model (The standardized habituation shape)

           data = data_q2_complete, REML = FALSE, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

# 1. Household Size (Main Effect)

anova(m0, m1)

To verify that these null results were not an artifact of model specification, we conducted a sensitivity analysis. We systematically compared the baseline model (m0) against expanded models incorporating each demographic factor (both as main effects and as interactions with trial number). As shown in our model comparison results, none of these additions yielded a statistically significant improvement in model fit, further reinforcing the robustness of the baseline habituation trajectory.

As a result, model comparison revealed that the baseline habituation model—incorporating natural splines (df=4) for trial number and accounting for hierarchical random intercepts—provided the most parsimonious fit to the data. The inclusion of demographic predictors, including household size, language background, and caregiver gender, did not significantly improve model fit. These findings suggest that the habituation trajectory is a robust developmental phenomenon, independent of the demographic variations assessed in this study. Furthermore, this model specification maintains internal consistency with the analytical frameworks established in Q1 and Q3, facilitating cross-question comparability.

To complement our statistical findings, we examined the habituation trajectories visually. This allows us to move beyond abstract numbers and see if the decline in looking time follows a simple linear path or if it exhibits the more complex, non-linear patterns identified in our models. Specifically, by comparing monolingual and bilingual infants in Figure 1, we can evaluate whether the process of habituation—the rate and shape of the decline—differs by language background.

2.6 Visualization of language group trajectories

# --- VISUALIZING HABITUATION BY LANGUAGE GROUP ---
# We compare the habituation curves of monolingual and bilingual infants.
# We use natural splines (df=4) to ensure the visual lines match the 
# statistical models we tested earlier.

ggplot(data_q2_complete, aes(x = testing_trial, y = looking_time, color = language_group)) +
# 1. Plot raw group means for each trial
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 2) +
# 2. Add the non-linear spline trend for each group
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              formula = y ~ splines::ns(x, df = 4), 
              se = TRUE, 
              alpha = 0.1) +
# 3. Label for clarity
    labs(
    x = "Trial Number",
    y = "Mean Looking Time (seconds)",
    color = "Language Group",
    title = "Habituation Trajectory by Language Group",
    subtitle = "Fitted with Natural Splines (df=4) to match statistical models"
  ) +
  # 4. Ensure each trial number is labeled on the x-axis
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:max(data_q2_complete$testing_trial)) +
  theme_minimal()

In Figure 1, the vertical distance between the teal and red curves indicates a baseline difference in total looking time between groups; however, because the curves are parallel, we conclude that the process of habituation—the rate at which infants lose interest—is identical for both monolingual and bilingual infants.

3 RQ3 - Methodological effects

Assess how methodological choices influence results.

  • 3.1 Do differences contribute to variability?
  • 3.2 Do they affect interpretation?
  • 3.3 Do they affect reliability?

This analysis investigates Research Question 3: “Do methodological and measurement choices influence the estimation and interpretation of infant habituation?”. We specifically examine the seating arrangement (caregiver_seat), comparing infants in a caregiver’s lap (89.5% of observations) to those sitting alone (10.3%).

The goal is to determine if seating affects habituation while accounting for infant age, the experimental method used (e.g., Eye-tracking vs. HPP vs. Single-screen), and project-level differences across ManyBabies 1, 3, and 4.

3.1 Data Preparation and Zero-Inflation Handling

As noted in the MB project sources, infant looking times are often zero-inflated. To address this and meet project requirements for standardized coefficients, we: 1. Filter trials: Focus only on valid testing trials (testing_trial > 0). 2. Clean seating: Remove “changed_throughout” (n=54) and missing values. 3. Log-transform: Create log_looking_time to handle skew. 4. Scale: Standardize age_days and testing_trial to produce \(\beta\) coefficients.

# Load the raw data
data <- read.csv("final_merged_manybabies.csv")

age_levels <- c(
  "< 3 months", "3–6 months", "6–9 months", "9–12 months",
  "12–15 months", "15–18 months", "18–21 months", "> 21 months"
)

data_rq3 <- data %>%
  # STEP A: Create testing trial
  dplyr::mutate(
    testing_trial = ifelse(trial_number > 0, trial_number, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  
  # STEP B: Create age variable
  dplyr::mutate(
    age_cut = cut(
      age_days,
      breaks = c(0, 90, 180, 270, 365, 455, 545, 635, Inf),
      labels = age_levels,
      right = FALSE
    ),
    age = dplyr::coalesce(
      as.character(age_group_new),
      as.character(age_cut)
    ),
    age = factor(age, levels = age_levels)
  ) %>%
  
  # STEP C: Collapse sparse age groups
  dplyr::mutate(
    age_group_clean = dplyr::case_when(
      as.character(age) %in% c("15–18 months", "18–21 months") ~ "15–21 months",
      TRUE ~ as.character(age)
    ),
    age_group_clean = factor(age_group_clean)
  ) %>%
  
  # STEP D: Filter data
  dplyr::filter(
    !trial_type %in% c("TRAIN", "fam"),
    !is.na(age),
    !is.na(looking_time),
    !is.na(caregiver_seat),
    caregiver_seat != "changed_throughout"
  ) %>%
  
  # STEP E: Final formatting
  dplyr::mutate(
    caregiver_seat = factor(
      caregiver_seat,
      levels = c("caregiver_lap_only", "seat_alone_only"),
      labels = c("Caregiver Lap", "Sitting Alone")
    ),
    method = factor(
      method,
      levels = c("eyetracking", "hpp", "singlescreen")
    ),
    trial_type = factor(trial_type),
    age_sc = as.numeric(scale(age_days)),
    trial_sc = as.numeric(scale(testing_trial)),
    household_size_z = as.numeric(scale(household_size)),
    log_lt = log1p(looking_time)
  )

3.3 Distribution Analysis: Checking for Confounds

A critical step in this analysis is determining whether caregiver seating is a truly independent variable or a proxy for other methodological choices. As noted in the sources, there is a significant structural imbalance in the ManyBabies dataset: infants sitting alone are heavily overrepresented in eyetracking data, while those on a caregiver’s lap are the standard in HPP and single-screen paradigms.

3.3.1 Visualizing the Structural Imbalance

The following visualizations assess how seating arrangements are distributed across the three ManyBabies projects, the various experimental methods, and infant age groups. These plots reveal whether “Sitting Alone” is clustered within specific technical or developmental contexts.

3.3.2 Quantifying Lab and Methodological Overlap

Beyond visual trends, we must statistically quantify the confounding between labs and seating. Because seating options are often fixed at the lab level, “Sitting Alone” might be confounded with unmeasured factors such as specialized equipment or researcher expertise in independent-sitting protocols.

This section identifies flexible labs (those using both seating types) to determine if the seating effect can be disentangled from lab identity.

# Quantify 'Flexible' vs. 'Fixed' Labs
lab_seating_summary <- data_rq3 %>%
  group_by(lab_id) %>%
  summarize(
    # Updated to match the labels created in Step E
    n_lap = sum(caregiver_seat == "Caregiver Lap"),
    n_alone = sum(caregiver_seat == "Sitting Alone"),
    total_trials = n(),
    # Identify labs that actually use both options
    is_flexible = n_lap > 0 & n_alone > 0
  )

# Calculate proportions for the report
total_labs <- nrow(lab_seating_summary)
flexible_labs_count <- sum(lab_seating_summary$is_flexible)
percent_flexible <- (flexible_labs_count / total_labs) * 100

cat("Out of", total_labs, "labs,", flexible_labs_count, 
    "(", round(percent_flexible, 1), "%) used both seating types.\n")
Out of 126 labs, 16 ( 12.7 %) used both seating types.
# Confirm Method-Seating Overlap
# Quantifies the percentage of 'Alone' sitters per measurement method
# This identifies the percentage of 'Alone' sitters per measurement method
method_overlap <- data_rq3 %>%
  group_by(method, caregiver_seat) %>%
  tally() %>%
  group_by(method) %>%
  mutate(percent = n / sum(n) * 100)
print(method_overlap)

3.4 Primary Visualization: Habituation Splines

This plot uses the Natural Spline (\(df=4\))—identified as the best-fitting functional form—to show the “rapid initial decrease and subsequent leveling off” of looking times.

ggplot(data_rq3, aes(x = testing_trial, y = looking_time, color = caregiver_seat, fill = caregiver_seat)) +
  # Raw data jittered with low alpha to show variance
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.05, width = 0.25, height = 0) + 
  
  # 95% CI Ribbons using the spline fit (df=4 is the best fit)
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ splines::ns(x, df = 4), se = TRUE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  
  # Formatting axes to show the whole scales dynamically
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1, max(data_rq3$testing_trial, na.rm = TRUE), by = 1)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    # Set breaks up to the actual max (e.g., 30s for MB4)
    breaks = seq(0, ceiling(max(data_rq3$looking_time, na.rm = TRUE)), by = 2)
  ) +
  
  # Aesthetic styling
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") + 
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(
    title = "Habituation Trajectories by Seating Arrangement",
    subtitle = "Natural Spline Model (df=4) showing Caregiver Lap (n=43,580) vs. Sitting Alone (n=5,037)",
    x = "Trial Number", 
    y = "Looking Time (seconds)",
    color = "Seating", 
    fill = "Seating"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom", 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

3.5 Statistical Models and Performance

3.5.1 Statistical model (random intercepts only)

The omnibus model tests how infants’ habituation trajectories (nonlinear change in looking over trials; ns(trial_sc, 4)) vary through two targeted three-way interactions: one between caregiver seating and experimental method, and another between caregiver seating and age. The model also incorporates trial_type as a fixed-effect control to account for systematic differences in baseline looking times across MB project-specific stimuli (e.g. social, non-social). This model also accounts for individual differences in overall looking time (unique_subject_identifier, random intercept only) and the multi-level structure of the data across projects (project_id) and labs (lab_id). This model converged.

# Statistical Model: Random Intercepts only
model_random_intercepts <- lmer(
  log_lt ~ ns(trial_sc, 4) * caregiver_seat * method + 
    ns(trial_sc, 4) * caregiver_seat * age_sc + 
    trial_type + 
    (1 | project_id) + 
    (1 | stimulus_id) +
    (1 | lab_id) +     
    (1 | unique_subject_identifier), 
  data = data_rq3,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# Summarize model
#summary(model_random_intercepts)

# Output Standardized Coefficients (Beta) 
# Standardized coefficients are required to compare the magnitude of methodological impacts
tab_model(model_random_intercepts, 
          show.std = TRUE, 
          title = "Standardized Model Estimates (Targeted Interactions)")

# EYETRACKING DEEP-DIVE MODEL

eye_data <- subset(data_rq3, method == "eyetracking")

eye_model <- lmer(
  log_lt ~ ns(trial_sc, 4) * caregiver_seat * age_sc +
    trial_type +
    (1 | project_id) +
    #(1 | stimulus_id) +
    (1 | lab_id) +
    (1 | unique_subject_identifier),
  data = eye_data,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# NB: To ensure model stability and convergence within the eyetracking subsample, the random effect of stimulus_id was removed here. This was justified by the omnibus model results, which showed that stimulus-level variance was negligible and that stimulus-category differences were already sufficiently captured by the trial_type fixed effect.
 
#summary(eye_model)

tab_model(eye_model, show.std = TRUE, 
          title = "Eyetracking Model: Seating × Age × Habituation")

3.6 Conclusion

In our mixed-effects model analysis, the fixed-effects coefficient for caregiver_seatSitting Alone was positive and significant (b = 0.18, β = 0.26, SE = 0.046, p < .001). This indicates that infants sitting alone showed higher log looking times than those on the caregiver’s lap at the reference level of the model.

The seating effect is highly dependent on the experimental paradigm. Post-hoc comparisons slicing the effect by method revealed that the advantage for sitting alone was significant exclusively within eyetracking studies (estimate = −0.149, z = −3.63, p =.0003) and absent in both HPP (p = .58) and single-screen (p = .70) paradigms. This pattern was further validated in a eyetracking only model, which yielded a even more pronounced seating effect (b = 0.28, β = 0.36, p < .001).

Within the eyetracking context, the seating effect was developmentally graded. Contrasts at three levels of standardized age showed that the looking time advantage for sitting alone was largest for younger infants (age -1SD: estimate = −0.297, p < .0001) and attenuated significantly for older infants (age +1SD: estimate = −0.160, p = .024). This might suggest that physical stabilization or independent seating could have more impact on attention before infants achieve greater postural and attentional control.

The seating effect was further qualified by its position within the habituation trajectory. Significant interactions between caregiver seating and the mid-session spline components in the omnibus model (ns(trial_sc,4)2: β = −0.11, p = .011; ns(trial_sc,4)3: β = −0.18, p = .014) indicate that the elevation in looking time for infants sitting alone is most pronounced in the early-to-middle portion of the trial sequence. However, habituation slope contrasts remained non-significant (ps > .27), confirming that seating affects the baseline level of looking (intercept elevation) rather than the rate of information processing (slope).

A noteworthy discovery in this exploratory analysis was the structural confounding between seating and lab identity. Diagnostic analysis revealed that 12.7% of the 126 participating labs (16 out of 126) utilized both “Caregiver Lap” and “Sitting Alone” protocols, while the remaining sites relied exclusively on a single seating arrangement. This confirms that seating is oftentimes a fixed methodological choice made at the lab level. As such, the differences reported here might reflect lab-to-lab differences in specialized equipment, such as specific eyetracker mounts, high-chairs, seats, or harnesses, as well as differing levels of researcher expertise in optimizing infant comfort and cooperation during the habituation procedure.

While our mixed-effects models account for lab-to-lab variability through random intercepts (where lab_id variance was 0.06), the high degree of structural imbalance across the dataset means we cannot entirely disentangle the physical impact of the seat from broader lab-specific characteristics. The reversal between the raw unadjusted data (where lap infants look longer) and the modeled estimates (where alone infants look longer) highlights the necessity of controlling for measurement method. Because “Sitting Alone” is heavily clustered in eyetracking (25.1% of trials) compared to HPP (1.7%), the “Sitting Alone” advantage only becomes visible once the systematic differences in data capture between eyetracking and human coding are resolved. Given these findings, researchers should consider seating arrangement as a methodological covariate in any analyses, particularly in eyetracking studies of infant attention. At the very least, we strongly encourage developmental researchers to consistently report the seating arrangements used for their samples to facilitate more accurate cross-study comparisons.
